item.title: Lightspeed Commerce reports US$4.2M Q2 loss, revenue up from year ago
item.description: Lightspeed Commerce Inc. reported a loss of US$4.2 million in its latest quarter compared with a loss of US$32.7 million a year ago.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: MONTREAL — Lightspeed Commerce Inc.’s share price dropped roughly 14 per cent on the heels of the company revealing its latest quarter brought a US$4.2 million loss. The commerce technology company’s share price fell to $13.77 after it revealed the loss, which compared with a $32.7 million hit a year ago. Despite reporting a loss, Lightspeed’s chief executive insisted Thursday that a recent pivot to more “upmarket” clients has put the company on the path to success. Dax Dasilva told analysts there are “clear signals that the merchants we are winning are higher quality and more deeply attached to our software.” Since Dasilva, Lightspeed’s founder, returned to the helm in 2024, the company has been working to refocus its client base around North American retail and European hospitality. On the retail front, it recently attracted apparel company Bombas, the Hockey Hall of Fame in Toronto and the International Spy Museum in Washington, D.C. Its newest hospitality clients include the McManus Pub Co. in the U.K., Domaine & Demeure’s luxury chateaus and restaurants and the Indie Group’s bars. Many of the businesses are the kind of large, sophisticated clients Lightspeed wants to lure in because they tend to buy more software. “Larger, more established customers drive higher software payments revenue, stay with us longer and are better positioned to benefit from Lightspeed’s more advanced feature sets,” Dasilva explained. “In general, they provide higher lifetime value.” His remarks dovetailed with the release of Lightspeed’s results, which are calculated in U.S. dollars. Its quarterly loss amounted to three cents US per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30 compared with a loss of 24 cents US per diluted share a year earlier. On an adjusted basis, it earned 17 cents US per share in its latest quarter compared with an adjusted profit of 16 cents US share a year ago. Revenue totalled US$323.8 million, up from US$319 million in the same quarter last year. Subscription revenue for the quarter reached US$97.8 million, up from US$93.5 million a year ago, while transaction-based revenue amounted to US$213.9 million, down from US$215.8 million in the same quarter last year. Hardware and other revenue was US$12.2 million, up from US$9.7 million. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026. By Tara Deschamps

item.title: S&P/TSX composite down nearly 500 points, U.S. stock markets also fall
item.description: Canada’s main stock index was down nearly 500 points, weighed down by losses in the technology and base metal sectors, while U.S. stocks also fell.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index was down nearly 500 points, weighed down by losses in the technology and base metal sectors, while U.S. stocks also fell in late-morning trading. The S&P/TSX composite index was down 476.02 points at 35,865.38 a day after stock markets in Canada and the United States posted big gains following the U.S. midterm elections that saw Democrats take control of Congress. In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 1,136.98 points at 52,219.14. The S&P 500 index was down 212.50 points at 7,476.12, while the Nasdaq composite was down 1,019.48 points at 24,717.03. The Canadian dollar traded for 71.44 cents US compared with 71.63 cents US on Wednesday. The December crude oil contract was up US$2.28 at US$90.40 per barrel. The December gold contract was up US$29.80 at US$4,102.80 an ounce. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

item.title: Share buybacks can add value for investors but can't 'rescue bad companies'
item.description: Share buybacks can lift returns or be a potential red flag, but finance experts say investors should look at the overall picture of how companies allocate their capital.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Share buybacks can lift returns or be a potential red flag, but finance experts say investors should look at the overall picture of how companies allocate their capital to determine for themselves. When companies buy back their own stock, they often cancel those securities, reducing the number of outstanding shares available for trading in the market. That spreads profits over fewer shares, which can boost earnings per share metrics come earnings season and potentially lift the company’s stock price. “Some of the best and worst investments over the past few decades were heavy buyers of their own stock. Buybacks magnify what’s already there; it can be better for shareholders and good for businesses, but can’t rescue bad companies from their ultimate fates,” said Theresa Shutt, chief investment officer at Harbourfront Wealth Management. “You really need to look at the business itself.” Shutt said that buyback programs return excess cash to shareholders, in a way that offers the company more flexibility compared with hiking its dividend, which commits the company to making those payments at regular intervals. When a buyback occurs, she said shareholders get a bigger ownership stake “without spending a dollar.” Markets often view buybacks as a positive. “It can provide support for the share price, that increases demand for the stock, and that can lift the valuation as well,” she said. But not all buyback programs benefit investors. She said some companies also use buybacks as a form of “financial engineering” to artificially lift earnings per share metrics. Investors should also take note if companies are cutting back on investments, research and development or staffing to pay for buybacks, Shutt said. Using debt to fund buybacks is also a potential red flag. Brian Madden, chief investment officer with First Avenue Investment Counsel, said that while organic growth is the “Holy Grail” of equity investing, not all companies are going to be able to deliver growth at eye-popping levels and may look for other ways to add value for shareholders. For example, he said some companies may generate a lot of cash but have limited opportunities to reinvest that money into their operations — so they could use a buyback to reward investors instead. “One alternative would be just to let the cash pile up on your balance sheet, but that’s not ideal in the same way that having idle cash in your brokerage account is not ideal for an individual investor,” Madden said. “It’s an opportunity cost, and the way the opportunity cost manifests for a company is idle cash doesn’t earn a return.” When a company announces a new buyback program, Madden said the first step for investors is to ask themselves, “Is this anything new?” “Many companies announce share buybacks every year … for large companies it is the norm that most of them will have a normal course issuer bid authorization, which gives them the right but not the obligation to repurchase their shares,” Madden said. He said a good exercise for investors is to go back and see if a company has announced previous share buyback authorizations and find out how much of its own stock the firm actually repurchased. On the other hand, companies deciding not to purchase their shares may have other priorities, Madden said. “You also have to think about the company’s other uses for cash. Is it wise and prudent for them to be buying back their shares now, do they have upcoming bonds that they need to refinance, or do they have big capital expenditure commitments that they need to make good on,” he said. Overall, he said investors should zoom out when considering the merits or downsides of a buyback program. “In a unified way it’s all about evaluating how the company is at capital allocation,” Madden said. --- Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

item.title: BCE reports Q3 profit down from year ago, revenue edged higher
item.description: BCE Inc. reported a third-quarter profit attributable to common shareholders of $630 million as its operating revenue rose 2.2 per cent from a year ago.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: BCE Inc. reported a third-quarter profit attributable to common shareholders of $630 million as its operating revenue rose 2.2 per cent from a year ago. The company says the profit amounted to 67 cents per share for the quarter ended Sept. 30. The result compared with a profit of $4.50 billion or $4.84 per share a year ago when the company sold its minority stake in Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment to rival Rogers Communications Inc. On an adjusted basis, BCE said it earned 74 cents per share in its latest quarter, down from an adjusted profit of 79 cents per share in the same quarter last year. Operating revenue totalled $6.18 billion, up from $6.05 billion a year earlier. Last month, BCE announced a deal to sell a 49.9 per cent stake of a new company that will own and operate its wireless towers to Quebec investment manager La Caisse for $2.45 billion. The company said business markets revenue — comprised of income from both telecom and AI services — was $1.12 billion in the quarter, up 9.2 per cent from $1.03 billion a year ago. It said that encompassed 41 per cent growth of AI-powered solutions revenue, driven by strong demand for its Ateko and Bell Cyber brands. On the telecom side, BCE had a net gain of 24,110 postpaid mobile phone subscribers in its third quarter, up from 11,511 net activations during the same period a year earlier. It said the year-over-year gain reflected more customers transitioning from prepaid service, new subscribers from reaching a long-term government-sector mobile services contract, and lower customer churn — a measure of subscribers who cancelled their service. Postpaid customer churn was 1.06 per cent, an improvement from 1.13 per cent a year ago and Bell’s lowest level for the third quarter in four years. Bell cited lower market activity and its continued focus on customer service and retention. “In the year since our Investor Day 2025, Bell’s Q3 results show responsible investment in key growth areas and steadfast execution of our long-term priorities,” said BCE president and CEO Mirko Bibic in a news release. “Fibre and wireless continue to drive growth.” BCE’s mobile phone average revenue per user was $57.07, down 1.7 per cent from $58.04 a year ago. It said that decrease was due to multiple factors, including the CRTC’s prohibition on certain customer fees, which took effect in June. The regulator’s ban on activation, cancellation and modification fees have been met with resistance from Bell, along with Rogers and Telus, which have each introduced fees that the CRTC said could violate the new ban. The CRTC is in the midst of a review and said that if it determines the companies have violated the rules, they could face monetary penalties of up to $10 million. Bell also cited lower overage revenue from customers subscribing to unlimited and larger capacity data plans, along with lower international roaming revenue as customers both travel less and increasingly subscribe to plans that include U.S. and international roaming. --- CTV News, CP24 and BNN Bloomberg are owned by Bell Media, which is a division of BCE. Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.
